summary: Specifies OCB, a shared-key block-cipher-based encryption scheme that provides confidentiality and authenticity for the data and authenticity for associated data. It is a product of the Crypto Forum Research Group.

plainLanguage.summary: OCB is a way of using a block cipher that encrypts the data and proves it has not been tampered with in a single pass. It can also check data that is sent in the clear, such as a network header. The RFC defines the algorithm exactly, and says plainly what an implementer must not do.

questions: what tag lengths does ocb support
subtitle: A mode of operation that encrypts and authenticates in one pass over a block cipher.

tldr.problem: Encryption and authentication are often bolted together from two separate mechanisms with two separate keys. That is easy to misuse, and it costs an extra pass over the data.
tldr.mechanism: OCB is an authenticated encryption mode with associated data. It wraps a block cipher that operates on 128-bit blocks, and the only other choice is how long the authentication tag should be. The RFC gives the full pseudocode for the hash of the associated data, for encryption and for decryption, plus nine named parameter sets built on AES.
tldr.outcome: It is an Informational RFC that is the product of the Crypto Forum Research Group. The mode is secure assuming the block cipher is secure, but the security degrades as more data is encrypted under one key, so the RFC sets a limit of 2^48 blocks per key and insists that a nonce is never reused.

facts.label: Block size required of the cipher

today: RFC 7253 is an Informational RFC published in May 2014. It has not been obsoleted or updated. It is the Crypto Forum Research Group's specification of OCB, and the nine parameter sets it defines are the ones registered with IANA.

sections.title: What OCB Is
sections.content:
Schemes for authenticated encryption provide confidentiality and authentication at the same time. The traditional way to get both is to meld separate encryption and authentication mechanisms, each with its own key. Integrated schemes intertwine what is needed for confidentiality and what is needed for authenticity. Treating authenticated encryption as a single cryptographic goal makes it less likely to be misused, and an integrated scheme can be significantly faster than composing the two separately.

When a scheme allows unencrypted data to be authenticated at the same time as a plaintext is encrypted and authenticated, it is an authenticated encryption with associated data scheme. Associated data is useful when, for example, a network packet has routing information in the clear and an encrypted payload.

OCB is an AEAD scheme that depends on a block cipher. This document fully defines the encryption and decryption apart from the choice of block cipher and the length of the authentication tag that is part of the ciphertext. The block cipher must have a 128-bit block size, and each choice of cipher and tag length is a different variant of OCB.

OCB uses a nonce N, which must be distinct for each invocation of the encryption operation, and it requires the associated data A to be specified, though it may be zero length. The plaintext P and the associated data A can have any bit length. The resulting ciphertext consists of a ciphertext core the same length as P plus an authentication tag, and this document treats the two as concatenated.

The mode uses on average about a + m + 1.02 block cipher calls, where a is the block length of the associated data and m the block length of the plaintext, with the nonce implemented as a counter; if the nonce is random then it uses a + m + 2 calls. If the associated data is fixed during a session then, after preprocessing, there is effectively no cost to authenticating it again, and the mode averages m + 1.02 calls. OCB needs a single key K for the underlying cipher. It is online, in that one need not know the length of the associated data or the plaintext to begin encrypting, nor the length of the associated data or the ciphertext to begin decrypting. It is parallelizable, since the bulk of the cipher calls can be done at the same time, and the work beyond the cipher calls is a small, fixed number of logical operations per call. It enjoys provable security: the mode is secure assuming the underlying block cipher is secure.

The version defined here is a refinement of two earlier schemes. The original was published in 2001 and was listed as an optional component in IEEE 802.11i, a second version was published in 2004 and specified in ISO 19772, and the scheme described here is the one called OCB3 in the 2011 paper describing the mode. The only difference is that the tag length is now encoded into the internally formatted nonce. OCB was originally the acronym for Offset Codebook but is now the algorithm's full name.
sections.plainLanguage: OCB encrypts and checks the data in one go, using a block cipher that works on 128-bit blocks. It works on a stream of data without needing to know the length up front, and it can check headers that are sent in the clear.

sections.title: Parameters and Named Parameter Sets
sections.content:
The algorithms need two global parameters: a block cipher operating on 128-bit blocks, and the length of the authentication tags in use. Specifying a block cipher implicitly defines three symbols. KEYLEN is the block cipher's key length in bits. ENCIPHER(K,P) is the block cipher function mapping a 128-bit plaintext block P to its corresponding ciphertext block under the KEYLEN-bit key K. DECIPHER(K,C) is the inverse function mapping a 128-bit ciphertext block C back to its plaintext block under the same key.

The TAGLEN parameter gives the length of the authentication tag used by OCB and may be any value up to 128. Greater values give greater assurance of authenticity, but the ciphertexts are then longer than their plaintexts by TAGLEN bits. As an example, with 128-bit tags and AES with 192-bit keys, KEYLEN is 192, ENCIPHER is the AES-192 cipher, DECIPHER is its inverse and TAGLEN is 128.

The RFC then names nine common parameter sets, one for each combination of AES-128, AES-192 and AES-256 with a tag length of 128, 96 or 64. The interface for authenticated encryption schemes defined in RFC 5116 requires certain constants for each named scheme, and for all nine OCB sets P_MAX, A_MAX and C_MAX are unbounded, N_MIN is 1 byte and N_MAX is 15 bytes. The sets using AES-128, AES-192 and AES-256 have K_LEN equal to 16, 24 and 32 bytes. Each ciphertext is longer than its plaintext by exactly TAGLEN bits, so an AEAD_AES_128_OCB_TAGLEN64 ciphertext is exactly 64 bits longer than its plaintext.
sections.plainLanguage: Two choices define a variant: which block cipher, and how long the tag is. The tag can be anything up to 128 bits, and each extra bit of tag makes the ciphertext longer by one bit.

sections.title: How the Algorithm Works
sections.content:
The RFC gives the mode as pseudocode in three functions. The first, HASH, handles the associated data. It takes the key K and the associated data A and returns a 128-bit sum. If an application has no associated data it should be treated as the empty string, and HASH conveniently always returns 128 zero bits for the empty string.

All three functions start by computing the same key-dependent values. L_* is the encryption of a 128-bit block of zeros under the key. L_$ is double(L_*), L_0 is double(L_$), and L_i is double(L_{i-1}) for every integer i greater than zero. The doubling operation shifts a 128-bit string left by one bit and, if the first bit was one, exclusive-ors in the constant 10000111 padded to 120 zero bits.

HASH treats the associated data as a sequence of 128-bit blocks, with a possibly empty final partial block A_*. It keeps a running offset, where Offset_i is the previous offset exclusive-ored with L_ntz(i), and a running sum, where Sum_i is the previous sum exclusive-ored with the encryption of the block exclusive-ored with the offset. A final partial block is padded with a one bit and zeros, exclusive-ored with an offset derived from L_*, and encrypted.

OCB-ENCRYPT takes the key, a nonce of no more than 120 bits, the associated data and the plaintext, and returns a ciphertext of the plaintext length plus TAGLEN bits. It forms an internal nonce from the tag length, the nonce and a one bit, then derives a top value by encrypting the first part of it and stretches that value into a 128-bit offset. The plaintext is treated as a sequence of 128-bit blocks in the same way. Each block gets its own offset from the same chain, and the ciphertext block is the offset exclusive-ored with the encryption of the plaintext block exclusive-ored with the offset. A checksum of the plaintext blocks is accumulated in parallel. A final partial block is exclusive-ored with a padded encryption and added to the checksum. The tag is the encryption of the checksum exclusive-ored with the offset and L_$, exclusive-ored with the result of HASH over the associated data. The output is the ciphertext blocks followed by the first TAGLEN bits of the tag.

OCB-DECRYPT takes the key, the nonce, the associated data and a ciphertext of at least TAGLEN bits, and returns either the plaintext or the signal INVALID, which indicates an authentication failure. It runs the same construction with the decryption function in place of the encryption function, computes its own tag, and compares the first TAGLEN bits with the tag that came with the ciphertext. If they match it returns the plaintext, and if they do not it returns INVALID.
sections.plainLanguage: Each block of the message gets a different one-time pad, drawn from a chain the key generates, and the same chain lets the receiver recover the message. A running checksum of the message plus a hash of the header produces the tag.

sections.title: Nonce Requirements
sections.content:
It is crucial that a nonce is not repeated. The inadvertent reuse of the same nonce by two encryptions with the same key but different plaintexts undermines the confidentiality of both plaintexts and undermines all of the authenticity and integrity protection that the key provides. OCB should therefore only be used where nonce uniqueness can be provided with certainty. It is acceptable to input the same nonce value multiple times to the decryption operation.

The consequences of reuse are serious if an attacker observes two ciphertexts created with the same nonce and key, unless the plaintext and associated data in both encryptions were identical. First, confidentiality is lost, because the attacker can infer relationships between the two plaintexts. Second, authenticity is lost, because the attacker can recover secret information used to provide authenticity, which makes later forgeries trivial. There are other AEAD schemes, particularly the Synthetic Initialization Vector scheme in RFC 5297, that suit environments where nonces are unavailable or unreliable. OCB is not such a scheme.

Nonces need not be secret, and a counter may be used for them. If two parties send OCB-encrypted plaintexts to each other using the same key, the space of nonces used by the two parties must be partitioned so that no nonce one party could use to encrypt could be used by the other, for example by using odd and even counters.
sections.plainLanguage: Never encrypt twice under the same key with the same nonce. If you do, an attacker who sees both ciphertexts can work out what the messages said and can forge later ones.

sections.title: Security Properties and Their Limits
sections.content:
OCB achieves two security properties. Confidentiality is defined as indistinguishability from random bits, meaning an adversary cannot tell OCB output from the same number of random bits. Authenticity is defined as authenticity of ciphertexts, meaning an adversary cannot produce a valid nonce and ciphertext pair that it has not already acquired. Both depend on the underlying block cipher being secure as a strong pseudorandom permutation, so OCB should be used with a conservatively designed, well trusted cipher such as AES. If the cipher is not secure in that sense, the guarantees vanish.

Both properties degrade as s squared over 2 to the 128, where s is the total number of blocks the adversary acquires. The proven security disappears once s reaches 2 to the 64, so a key should never be used to generate a number of ciphertext blocks near or beyond that. To keep the degradation small, a given key should be used to encrypt at most 2 to the 48 blocks, which is 2 to the 55 bits or 4 petabytes, including the associated data. Automated key management is recommended in systems exchanging large amounts of data, as set out in RFC 4107.

When a ciphertext decrypts as INVALID, it is the implementor's responsibility to make sure that no information beyond that fact is made adversarially available.

OCB produces an internal 128-bit authentication tag, and TAGLEN decides how many bits of it travel with the ciphertext and are used for authentication. A longer tag means an adversary can trivially forge with less probability, and makes the ciphertext TAGLEN bits longer. It is up to the application designer to choose the value, and long tags cost no more computationally than short ones. Normally a given key should be used to create ciphertexts with a single tag length, and an application should reject any ciphertext that claims authenticity under the same key but a different tag length. The ciphertext core and all the bits of the tag do depend on the tag length, but that is done for added robustness to misuse and does not mean receivers should accept variable tag lengths under one key.

Timing attacks are not part of the formal security model, and an implementation should mitigate them where that is a concern. The time taken to encrypt or decrypt a string should not depend on the key or the contents of the string. The only explicitly conditional operation that depends on private data is the doubling function, so constant-time implementations of the block cipher and of doubling remove most, if not all, sources of timing attacks. Power-usage attacks are likewise out of scope of the formal model. The scheme also reveals the length of the plaintext in the ciphertext, and where that is valuable information to hide, techniques beyond OCB, typically padding, are necessary.
sections.plainLanguage: The security holds only if the underlying cipher is sound, and it weakens slowly as more data is encrypted under one key, so the RFC caps how much a single key may protect. The code must also run in constant time, and the length of the message is visible.

sections.title: IANA Considerations
sections.content: IANA has defined a registry for Authenticated Encryption with Associated Data parameters, and the RFC adds nine entries to it, one for each named parameter set. The AEAD_AES_128 sets have numeric identifiers 20, 21 and 22 for tag lengths of 128, 96 and 64, the AEAD_AES_192 sets have 23, 24 and 25, and the AEAD_AES_256 sets have 26, 27 and 28. Each entry refers back to the parameter set defined in the RFC.
sections.plainLanguage: The nine combinations of cipher and tag length now have numbers in the IANA registry, so a protocol can name the one it wants.

items.title: One pass
items.text: About a + m + 1.02 block cipher calls for a block length of a for the associated data and m for the plaintext.

items.title: Online
items.text: You need not know the length of the associated data or the plaintext before you start encrypting.

items.title: Parallelizable
items.text: The bulk of the block cipher calls can be carried out at the same time.

items.title: Provable security
items.text: The mode is secure assuming the underlying block cipher is secure.

items.title: Headers are checked too
items.text: Unencrypted associated data can be authenticated at the same time as the plaintext is encrypted.
